support.reconciliation: The tradition reads its texts through a fixed line of authority. Bahá'u'lláh's writings are scripture (Tier 1, accepted by every Bahá'í group). ʿAbdu'l-Bahá is the authorised interpreter, and his writings are counted as primary (corpus.md; METHOD.md section 9, decision 4). Shoghi Effendi is the next authorised interpreter (Tier 2). The Universal House of Justice explains and legislates where the texts leave matters open (Tier 2); under decision 8 it can make a result unclear but cannot decide one. On killing, the hard texts reconcile as follows. (1) Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶19 forbids murder without exception or class of victim. ¶62 sets death, or life imprisonment, for deliberate murder and arson. The tradition places ¶62 wholly with institutions: Notes 86 and 87 (House of Justice, quoting Shoghi Effendi; verified by search in an earlier session) leave degrees of the offence and the choice of penalty to the House of Justice. ʿAbdu'l-Bahá (Some Answered Questions, chapter on the punishment of criminals; counted; verified by search in an earlier session) teaches that the individual has no right of vengeance and should forgive, while the community may punish to protect people and not out of revenge. So ¶62 is a court matter (exclusion (a)), and the tradition does not dispute this. (2) The Báb's harsher ordinances, including holy war, are held superseded. Bahá'u'lláh declared the law of holy war "blotted out from the Book" (Lawḥ-i-Bishárát, Tier 1, verified by search in earlier sessions). ʿAbdu'l-Bahá is quoted in the Notes to the Aqdas as saying the Bayán stands only where the Aqdas confirms it (not re-checked). corpus.md makes the Báb's laws supporting, not decisive, on conduct. (3) The strongest sanction against internal opponents is shunning of declared Covenant-breakers (Will and Testament, counted), which limits fellowship but never permits harm. (4) Self-defence against an individual attacker is reportedly allowed in letters written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi (Tier 2, unverified), which matches K1's exception. (5) A wider ban on striking anyone (¶148) is read by the House of Justice (letter of 24 January 1993, Tier 2, mainstream) as allowing gentle physical discipline of children. That reading concerns light correction only and leaves the ban on killing untouched. No counted text found lets any private person, including a parent, husband, master, crowd or zealot, kill anyone.

K1.label: Taught
K1.reason: Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶19 (Tier 1, every group) explicitly forbids murder and names no class of victim, so it reaches everyone K1 protects, newborns included (rules 7 and 9). ¶148 (no striking, no contention) and Gleanings LXVI (any soul) add wider duties. ʿAbdu'l-Bahá (counted) denies any private person a right of vengeance. No counted text found lets a private person kill. The death penalty of ¶62 is a court matter that the tradition's own texts place with institutions (rule 5; not disputed, so rule 6 does not apply), holy war was abolished (Lawḥ-i-Bishárát), and the Báb's laws are not decisive under corpus.md and are held superseded. Caveat: every verified row was verified by search in earlier project sessions (13 October 2026), not in this run, because no search was possible; ¶19 was seen only on Bahai Library Online, a mirror of the authorised text. ¶19 must be read directly on bahai.org/library before admission (METHOD.md section 3).

K0.label: Taught
K0.reason: Follows a fortiori from Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶19 (rule 7). The counted chapter of Some Answered Questions also states explicitly that no individual may take revenge and that the wronged should forgive. The Will and Testament (counted) asks believers to be a salve to those who wound them. Nothing found permits killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge. The same verification caveat as for K1 applies.

K3.label: Silent
K3.reason: No counted text was found that addresses sparing non-combatants (children, the old, civilians, those who surrender) in war. Bahá'u'lláh abolished holy war (Lawḥ-i-Bishárát, verified by search earlier), which removes religious war altogether but says nothing about conduct within a defensive or collective war. Gleanings CXIX (collective action against an aggressor) and CXXXIX (annulling the rule of the sword) are unverified leads. Nothing found permits killing non-combatants, so the support is Implied at most. Not searched in this run.

counter.reconciliation: How the tradition reads its own hard texts, with the standing of each authority. (1) Bahá'u'lláh's writings are scripture (Tier 1, accepted by every Bahá'í group). The Kitáb-i-Aqdas forbids killing outright (¶19) and forbids contention, conflict and striking another (¶148). Its one provision for taking life is the penal law of ¶62 (death or, as a permitted alternative, life imprisonment for deliberate murder and arson). (2) 'Abdu'l-Bahá, the authorised interpreter, whose writings the tradition holds to be part of its sacred text (counted, all branches), separates the individual from the community: the individual has no right to vengeance and should forgive, while the community may punish to protect its members, without hatred (Some Answered Questions, ch. 77). So ¶62 gives no private person, kinsman or avenger any right to kill; it is a court matter, context only under rule 5. 'Abdu'l-Bahá also states that the laws of the Báb's Bayán are superseded except where the Aqdas confirms them (as quoted in the 1992 Aqdas volume), and Bahá'u'lláh releases believers from the Bayán's ordinance on books (¶77) and declares the law of holy war "blotted out from the Book" (Lawḥ-i-Bishárát, Tier 1). The harshest texts in the wider canon, the Báb's ordinances against unbelievers (Tier 1 but flagged as supporting, not decisive; exact loci unverified), are therefore not Bahá'í law. (3) Shoghi Effendi, the Guardian and next authorised interpreter (Tier 2; binding on the mainstream and on groups that accept the Guardianship), states that life imprisonment is a permitted alternative under ¶62 (Note 87). Letters on his behalf, recalled but not verified, allow defence against robbers and discourage armed resistance to religious persecution. (4) The Universal House of Justice, the elected body the tradition treats as authorised to elucidate and legislate (Tier 2; under METHOD.md section 9, decision 8, it can make a result unclear but never decides one), leaves the details of ¶62 (degrees of offence, extenuating circumstances, which penalty is the norm, how it is carried out) to its own future legislation and presents the penal laws as intended for a future state of society (Notes 86 and 87). Its 1993 letter forbids any husband to beat his wife and condemns child abuse. It does not narrow ¶19 in any way found. (5) Other apparent hard cases: ¶37's warning that God will send one who deals mercilessly with a false claimant is divine retribution, not a human licence (rule 4; unverified). The shunning of Covenant-breakers in 'Abdu'l-Bahá's Will is withdrawal of company, paired in the same text with kindliness to all peoples, friends or strangers. The killing of three Azalís by some of Bahá'u'lláh's followers in 'Akká in 1872 is, in the tradition's own history (God Passes By), condemned by Bahá'u'lláh as conduct that made his heart and pen groan (unverified; Azali and some academic accounts dispute his role, which is a historical question, not a text). No counted text was found that permits a private person to kill a non-attacker, that permits killing newborns or children, that declares any killing blameless because of the victim's status or act, that limits the protection of life to Bahá'ís, or that grades it by status.

K1.label: Taught
K1.reason: Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶19 (Tier 1, all branches, Explicit, VERIFIED (search) in earlier project research) forbids killing with no class of victim excepted (rule 7). 'Abdu'l-Bahá (Some Answered Questions ch. 77, counted for all branches) denies any private person the right to kill, even in revenge for murder, and gives punishment to the community, so the one penal killing in the texts (¶62) is a court matter, context only (rule 5), and no text extends it to a private agent; no dispute within the tradition on this was found, so rule 6 does not apply. Wider bans reach every class K1 protects: striking anyone (¶148), striking a child ('Abdu'l-Bahá, Selections 95; rule 9), slavery (¶72), followers of other religions (¶144; holy war abolished). Counter-evidence searched for: none of the counted texts found permits private killing, infanticide, blameless killing by status, or in-group-only protection (rules 2 and 3 not met). ¶37 is divine retribution (rule 4, Implied, unverified). The Báb's severe ordinances are flagged as not decisive (rule 1), held superseded by counted texts, and their loci are unverified. Caveat: every VERIFIED row rests on search checks from 2026-10-13; nothing could be rechecked in this run, and ¶19 was confirmed only on a mirror of the authorised text, so it needs direct reading on bahai.org before an article can be admitted.

K0.label: Taught
K0.reason: ¶19 (Tier 1, Explicit) forbids killing whatever the motive, which includes killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge (rule 7). 'Abdu'l-Bahá (Some Answered Questions ch. 77, counted, all branches) states outright that the wronged individual has no right to vengeance and should forgive, and calls retaliation blameworthy (Explicit for the revenge clause). ¶148 forbids contention, conflict and striking another (wider rule). No counted text found permits a killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge; ¶62 is a court penalty (rule 5) that the tradition's own authorities separate from private vengeance.

K3.label: Silent
K3.reason: No counted text found addresses whether people who are not fighting may be killed in war (rule 8). The counted texts on war are context only (rule 5): the law of holy war is "blotted out from the Book" (Lawḥ-i-Bishárát, verified), and, as recalled but unverified, Bahá'u'lláh calls the rulers to rise together against any one of them who takes up arms (Gleanings CXIX, collective security). The general ban on killing in ¶19 is not stated to govern conduct in war, and the tradition accepts collective force against an aggressor, so reading ¶19 as teaching K3 would be Implied only. 'Abdu'l-Bahá's writings and talks on war were not searched for a passage on sparing non-combatants; if one is found in his writings (counted), this could move to Taught.

verified.reconciliation: The tradition reads its texts through a fixed line of authority. Bahá'u'lláh's writings are scripture (Tier 1, accepted by every Bahá'í group). ʿAbdu'l-Bahá is the authorised interpreter, and his authenticated writings are counted as primary (corpus.md; METHOD.md section 9, decision 4). Shoghi Effendi is the next authorised interpreter (Tier 2). The Universal House of Justice elucidates and legislates where the texts leave matters open (Tier 2, mainstream branch). Under decision 8 it can make a result unclear but cannot decide one. On killing: (1) Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶19 forbids murder with no class of victim excepted (verified by search in an earlier session, on a mirror of the authorised text). ¶73, as recalled but not verified, forbids any soul to slay another. ¶148 forbids striking anyone. (2) The one provision for taking life is the penal law of ¶62 (death or life imprisonment for deliberate murder and arson). The tradition places it wholly with institutions. ʿAbdu'l-Bahá (Some Answered Questions, chapter on the punishment of criminals; counted; verified earlier) teaches that the individual has no right to vengeance and should forgive, while the community may punish without hatred to protect its members. Notes 86 and 87 (House of Justice, quoting Shoghi Effendi; verified earlier) leave degrees of guilt and the choice of penalty to the House of Justice. No reading of ¶62 as a licence for a kinsman or private avenger was found, so it is a court matter under rule 5, and rule 6 does not apply. (3) The Báb's harsher ordinances, including holy war, are held superseded. Bahá'u'lláh declared the law of holy war 'blotted out from the Book' (Lawḥ-i-Bishárát, Tier 1, verified earlier). ʿAbdu'l-Bahá states that the Bayán stands only where the Aqdas confirms it (as quoted in the 1992 Aqdas volume, verified earlier). ¶77's release from the ordinance on books is unverified. corpus.md makes the Báb's laws supporting, not decisive, on conduct, and no Bábí text letting a private person kill has been identified. (4) The strongest sanction the counted texts set against internal opponents is the shunning of Covenant-breakers (Will and Testament, verified earlier). The same text commands kindliness to friends and strangers and asks believers to be a salve to those who wound them. (5) Zealot killings: the tradition's own history (God Passes By, unverified here) records Bahá'u'lláh condemning his followers' killing of three Azalís in 1872, and its texts are recalled as disowning the 1852 attempt on the Shah. Azalí and some academic accounts dispute his role; that is history, not text. (6) Self-defence against an individual attacker is reportedly allowed, and armed resistance to religious persecution discouraged, in letters written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi (Tier 2, unverified). This matches or is stricter than K1's exception. (7) The House of Justice's 1993 letter reads the ban on striking as allowing gentle discipline of children, forbids any husband to beat his wife and condemns child abuse. It touches light correction only, not killing. No counted text found lets any private person (parent, husband, master, crowd, zealot or kinsman) kill anyone. None limits the protection of life to Bahá'ís or grades it by status, and none prescribes death for apostasy or heresy.

K1.label: Taught
K1.reason: Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶19 (Tier 1, every branch, Explicit) forbids murder and names no class of victim, so it reaches everyone K1 protects, newborns included (rules 7 and 9). ʿAbdu'l-Bahá (Some Answered Questions, chapter on the punishment of criminals; counted for every branch; Clear teaching) denies any private person the right to kill, even in revenge for murder. So the one penal killing in the texts (¶62) is a court matter, context only (rule 5). No dispute about its judicial character was found within the tradition, so rule 6 does not apply. Wider duties support the scope: ¶148 (no striking anyone) and Selections no. 95 (no striking a child). ¶72 (no slave trade), ¶144 (amity with all religions) and the abolition of holy war are Implied only. Counter-evidence: no counted, verified text permits private killing, infanticide, blameless killing because of who the victim is, or protection limited to one's own community (rules 2 and 3 not met). ¶37 is divine retribution (rule 4; unverified). The Báb's ordinances are flagged as not decisive, held superseded by counted texts, and their loci are unverified. Caveat: every VERIFIED row rests on search checks recorded in earlier sessions (13 October 2026). None could be re-searched in this run, because the search budget was used up and direct fetches fail. ¶19 has been seen only on a mirror of the authorised text. The label stands on the project's recorded verification and must be confirmed by reading ¶19 directly (and ideally ¶73) on bahai.org/library before admission (decision 6).

K0.label: Taught
K0.reason: Follows a fortiori from Kitáb-i-Aqdas ¶19 (Tier 1, Explicit, rule 7), which forbids killing whatever the motive. ʿAbdu'l-Bahá (Some Answered Questions, counted, every branch) states outright that the wronged individual has no right to vengeance, should forgive, and that retaliation is blameworthy (Explicit for the revenge clause). The Will and Testament (counted) asks believers to be a salve to those who wound them. No counted text found permits killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge; ¶62 is a court penalty that the tradition's own authorities separate from private vengeance (rule 5). The same verification caveat as for K1 applies.

K3.label: Silent
K3.reason: No counted text found addresses whether people who are not fighting may be killed in war (rule 8). The counted texts on war are context only (rule 5). The law of holy war is 'blotted out from the Book' (Lawḥ-i-Bishárát, verified earlier). That abolishes religious war but says nothing about conduct within a war that does happen (Implied). As recalled but unverified, Bahá'u'lláh calls the rulers to rise together against any one of them who takes up arms (Gleanings CXIX). So the tradition does not read its general ban on killing (¶19, and ¶73 if verified) as ruling out all war, and applying that ban to non-combatants in war is Implied only. ʿAbdu'l-Bahá's writings on war (for example The Secret of Divine Civilization) were not searched; a passage there on sparing non-combatants could move this to Taught. This label depends on how the project treats general bans on killing for K3 in other traditions; see the fairness notes.

verified.branch_notes: The K1 and K0 labels rest on Bahá'u'lláh's writings (Tier 1) and ʿAbdu'l-Bahá's authenticated writings (counted). Every Bahá'í group accepts these: the mainstream community under the Universal House of Justice, and the small groups that reject it, such as those descended from Mason Remey's claim. So the labels hold for every branch. The Will and Testament is accepted by the mainstream and the Remey-derived groups. A small 'Free Bahá'í' current that disputed it is not treated as a living branch, and this was not checked; only the support and limit rows on the Will depend on it, not the labels. Notes 86 and 87, the 1993 letter and the abortion letters (Universal House of Justice) bind only the mainstream branch, and are reconciliation or context only. Letters written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi bind the mainstream and Guardian-accepting groups; they are Tier 2 and unverified here. Azalís (Bayánís) accept the Báb's writings but reject Bahá'u'lláh; they are a separate Bábí movement, not a Bahá'í branch, and their texts were not assessed. Not checked: how the Remey-derived groups read ¶62 or the self-defence guidance, and whether any group reads ¶62 as a private licence (none is known).
verified.fairness_notes: 1. The Báb's writings are Tier 1 but flagged in corpus.md as 'supporting, not decisive' on conduct, so even a harsh Bábí text could not make K1 Contradicted. To an adherent of an older tradition this can look lighter than the treatment of, for example, the Hebrew Bible's laws for Christians, which are counted and then reconciled. The flag rests on the tradition's own Tier 1 and counted texts declaring the Bayán superseded (Lawḥ-i-Bishárát; ʿAbdu'l-Bahá's statement). No Bábí text licensing private killing has been found, so the flag changes no label now. Even so, the Bayán and the Qayyúm al-Asmá' should be checked as if counted and superseded, to show that the result does not depend on the flag. 2. The Bahá'í texts date from 1844 to 1921, after many legal systems had moved killing and punishment into courts. Their lack of hard texts partly reflects when they were written. The clean result should not be read as a comparison of traditions' moral worth. 3. ¶62's plural 'ye' is treated as a court matter on the strength of ʿAbdu'l-Bahá and the Notes. The same rule 5 test (does a counted text name a kinsman or private agent?) must be applied to other traditions' penal texts, for example the blood-avenger of Numbers 35 or the heirs' role in qiṣāṣ. In the Bahá'í case no counted text names a private agent. 4. The zealot case (1872) is reconciled through the tradition's own history (God Passes By). Azalí and some academic accounts dispute it, so a critic could say the tradition is judging its own case. A row now records that dispute, and nothing decides on it. 5. K3 is Silent although the founder abolished holy war outright. Silent means only that no counted text addresses non-combatants, not that killing them is allowed. If another tradition's general ban on killing (for example ahiṃsā) is credited as teaching K3 through a wider rule, the same reading must be weighed for ¶19 and ¶73. The difference cited here is that the Bahá'í texts accept collective force against an aggressor, but that text (Gleanings CXIX) is itself unverified. 6. Every Bahá'í row rests on search checks from earlier sessions; none was re-checked in this run because the search budget was used up. That should count neither for nor against the tradition, and the same caveat must be applied to any other tradition checked under the same limit. 7. ¶19's English 'murder' (like the English rendering of the Hebrew lo tirtzach) could be said to assume a separate list of lawful killings. It should be read the same way across traditions: as covering every killing that the tradition's counted texts do not themselves set apart.
